picks.headline: Unsealed Files Show Open AI/Microsoft Knew Copying Was Illegal and Could Hurt Authors
picks.excerpt: Newly unsealed comments made in briefs filed by Open AI and Microsoft reveal that executives knew they were illegally training their products on copyrighted books and that AI generated books would likely displace human-authored books in the market.
picks.rationale: Freshest and heaviest item in the pool: internal admissions, now on the record, that the training copies were known to be unlawful and that AI books would displace human-authored ones — the exact market-harm prong the authors' summary-judgment fight turns on.
picks.framing_note: WRITER: lead on the BOOKS half — the unsealed defendant briefs about copyrighted books and displacement of human-authored titles. Do NOT re-tell the news-publisher/NYT clickthrough revelations: that unredaction already shipped on 2026-09-18 as books-ms-scraping-filings (TechCrunch, 'largest theft of labor in human history'). One clause of setup at most.

picks.headline: Industry bodies criticise government's "opt-out" AI proposals
picks.excerpt: The Australian Publishers Association (APA) and the Australian Society of Authors (ASA) have criticised proposals put forward by the Australian Government that would make the inclusion of Australian creative work in AI training opt-out by default. "We cannot shift the burden to creators and rights-holders to try to protect their work."
picks.rationale: A second national government moving to a default opt-out for AI training — the policy shape that decides whether any licensing market exists, with both the publisher and author bodies on record against it.
picks.framing_note: WRITER: this is the dedicated article; the same APA/ASA criticism also leads the Books+Publishing daily roundup (340842), which was dropped as a within-pool duplicate. Use only this one.

picks.headline: Accelerating Generative AI Integration in Libraries — Information Technology and Libraries, Vol. 45 No. 3 (2026)
picks.excerpt: A new special issue of Information Technology and Libraries is now available online. This special issue is devoted to "showcasing examples and ideas for integrating GenAI tools into galleries, libraries, archives, and museums."
picks.rationale: A whole peer-reviewed issue of worked GenAI implementations for galleries, libraries, archives and museums — open access, and the most directly copyable set of examples anyone running a collection can take to their own stack this week.
picks.framing_note: WRITER: name two or three concrete articles from the issue rather than describing 'a special issue' in the abstract.

picks.headline: Writing Conferences Shouldn't Ignore AI in Their Programming
picks.excerpt: Conference attendees have many questions about AI, and organizers would better serve their audience by engaging with intent and clarity.
picks.rationale: The one item aimed at the people who set the agenda for working writers — how to put AI on a conference programme on purpose instead of ducking it, which is where most authors will actually get their first briefing.
picks.framing_note: WRITER: Jane Friedman's posts are partly paywalled; keep to what the public portion supports and say so if the body is truncated.

picks.headline: Revisiting Vikram Chandra's Ode to the Art of Human Coding in the Age of AI
picks.excerpt: Twelve years ago, Vikram Chandra's Geek Sublime: The Beauty of Code, The Code of Beauty was published. In terms of actual history, that isn't long at all; in terms of technology, it's an eternity.
picks.rationale: The reading-side card in a policy-heavy five: a novelist's aesthetics of handwritten code re-read against generated code, and the only pick that argues about craft rather than contracts.
picks.framing_note: WRITER: this is an essay, not news — build the card around the specific claim the piece makes about Chandra's book, not around a general 'AI and creativity' theme.
